newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan aiming to speed up futures market launch.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan aiming to speed up futures market launch.

text.p: Regulators pledged on Tuesday to open Taiwan's long-awaited futures exchange in July 1997 -- months earlier than planned -- to stave off intense competitive pressure from the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME).

The exchange was originally scheduled to open in late 1997, but the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) had decided to move the target date forward to July, a commission official quoted chairman Lu Tung-ying as saying.
"July is a tight schedule for Taiwan, but we must have a local futures market to monitor the trading," Lee Chi-hsien, an official at the commission's futures department, told Reuters by telephone.
Taiwan's move was forced by the CME's plan to list derivatives linked to Taiwan's stock market index in November, brokers said.
The CME contracts would be the first futures and options to be based on Taiwan's stock index.

The SEC's chairman visited CME officials in Chicago in late September to explore ways of delaying the launch of the futures. But his efforts appeared to have failed, said Han Kai-ming, president of the Taipei Futures Association.

Taiwan could lose a potentially large market for stock-linked derivatives to Chicago if the CME listed its index futures first, said brokers. On the plus side, the CME move could shorten the preparation period for the island's futures exchange, they added.
"If not for the pressure from CME, it might take another two to three years before Taiwan opens its futures exchange," said one futures broker, who declined to be named.
Taiwan's parliament is expected to pass a futures trading law by the end of the year, providing a legal basis for trading, the SEC's Lee said.
